claims.claim: Jesus's crucifixion is usually dated AD 30 or 33, under Pontius Pilate.
claims.source: Standard; e.g. J. P. Meier, A Marginal Jew I (1991); Tacitus, Annals XV.44.

claims.claim: Acts is the second volume of Luke's work (Acts 1:1, Luke 1:1-4); Irenaeus about AD 180 names Luke as author.
claims.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.1.1; III.14.1.

claims.claim: Most scholars date Acts about AD 80-90; some to the 60s; some (Pervo) to 110-120.
claims.source: R. Pervo, Dating Acts (2006); standard introductions (e.g. R. E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, 1997).

claims.claim: Politarchs of Thessalonica, Gallio's proconsulship (about 51-52, Delphi inscription published 1905), and the 'first man' of Malta are confirmed by inscriptions.
claims.source: C. Hemer, The Book of Acts in the Setting of Hellenistic History (1989); the Gallio inscription (Bourguet, 1905).

claims.claim: Acts names more than a hundred people.
claims.source: Hemer (1989); PLEASE CHECK the exact count.

claims.claim: James the Lord's brother was executed in AD 62.
claims.source: Josephus, Antiquities XX.200.

claims.claim: James son of Zebedee killed by Herod Agrippa I about AD 44.
claims.source: Acts 12:1-2; Agrippa I died 44 (Josephus, Antiquities XIX.343-350).

claims.claim: 1 Clement (about AD 96) refers to the deaths of Peter and Paul.
claims.source: 1 Clement 5.

claims.claim: Views of Jesus's brothers: Jerome (about 383) cousins; Protevangelium of James (2nd c.) sons of Joseph; Luther and Calvin held Mary's perpetual virginity.
claims.source: Jerome, Against Helvidius; Protevangelium of James 9.2; standard histories of Mariology.

claims.claim: Pentecost (Feast of Weeks) fifty days after Passover; Acts gives 3,000 and 5,000.
claims.source: Leviticus 23:15-16; Acts 2:41; 4:4.

claims.claim: Paul: from Tarsus, Benjamite, Pharisee, Roman citizen by birth, trained under Gamaliel, tent-maker.
Stephen's death and Paul's conversion are usually dated AD 31-36; Aretas IV died about AD 40.
claims.source: Galatians 1:18; 2:1; 2 Corinthians 11:32; R. Jewett, A Chronology of Paul's Life (1979); R. Riesner, Paul's Early Period (1998).

claims.claim: Seven letters of Paul are undisputed; thirteen bear his name.
claims.source: Standard (e.g. Brown, Introduction, 1997).

claims.claim: 'Cemetery' from Greek koimeterion, sleeping place.
claims.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'cemetery'.

claims.claim: N. T. Wright linked Paul's going to Arabia with Elijah's journey to Horeb.
claims.source: N. T. Wright, 'Paul, Arabia, and Elijah (Galatians 1:17)', JBL 115 (1996) 683-692.

claims.claim: Stendahl (1976): 'call rather than conversion'; Segal (1990): Paul as convert.
claims.source: K. Stendahl, Paul Among Jews and Gentiles (1976); A. Segal, Paul the Convert (1990).

claims.claim: Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.
claims.source: Augustine, Sermon 382.4 (often cited); PLEASE CHECK the sermon number.

claims.claim: The church in China grew fastest after missionaries left in 1949.
claims.source: Common in histories of Chinese Christianity (e.g. D. Aikman, Jesus in Beijing, 2003); PLEASE CHECK, or soften.

claims.claim: Paul's journeys and dates (about 46-62); death under Nero by tradition.
claims.source: Acts 13-28; Eusebius, Church History II.22, 25; standard chronologies.

claims.claim: Claudius expelled Jews from Rome 'impulsore Chresto', usually dated AD 49.
claims.source: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Orosius VII.6.15; Acts 18:2.

claims.claim: Rome's Jewish catacomb inscriptions name at least eleven synagogues.
claims.source: H. J. Leon, The Jews of Ancient Rome (1960); PLEASE CHECK the number (11-13 are cited).

claims.claim: Last word of Acts is akolytos, 'unhindered'.
claims.source: Greek text, Acts 28:31.

claims.claim: Phoebe is called diakonos and prostatis; she probably carried Romans.
claims.source: Romans 16:1-2; standard commentaries (e.g. R. Jewett, Romans, Hermeneia, 2007).

claims.claim: Junia is a woman's name; Chrysostom took her as an apostle; Burer and Wallace argue 'well known to the apostles'.
claims.source: John Chrysostom, Homily 31 on Romans; E. J. Epp, Junia (2005); M. Burer and D. Wallace, NTS 47 (2001).

claims.claim: Ten women among those named or greeted in Romans 16 (Phoebe, Prisca, Mary, Junia, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus's mother, Julia, Nereus's sister).
claims.source: Romans 16:1-15, counted.

claims.claim: Rufus possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene.
claims.source: Mark 15:21; commentaries; flagged as possible only.

claims.claim: Origen argued God united the world under Rome to let the gospel spread.
claims.source: Origen, Against Celsus II.30.

claims.claim: Dura-Europos house church converted about AD 240, oldest known church building.
claims.source: C. H. Kraeling, The Christian Building (1967); usually dated 232/3-256.

claims.claim: Stark's model: 1,000 in 40, about 40% a decade, about 6.3 million by 300 and 33.9 million by 350, empire about 60 million; Mormon comparison.
claims.source: R. Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996), ch. 1, table 1.1.

claims.claim: Hopkins reached similar estimates.
claims.source: K. Hopkins, 'Christian Number and its Implications', JECS 6 (1998) 185-226.

claims.claim: The Roman church in 251 supported over 1,500 widows and needy.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History VI.43.11 (letter of Cornelius).

claims.claim: Gibbon's five secondary causes.
claims.source: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 15 (1776).

claims.claim: Hurtado: Christianity distinctive (exclusive, translocal, bookish, ethical).
claims.source: L. Hurtado, Destroyer of the Gods (2016).

claims.claim: Didache rediscovered by Philotheos Bryennios in 1873 in a manuscript of 1056 copied by Leon, published 1883; now in the Jerusalem Patriarchate library.
claims.source: Codex Hierosolymitanus 54; standard introductions (e.g. Milavec 2003). PLEASE CHECK the scribe's name.

claims.claim: Didache probably Syria, AD 50-120; parts may be as early as Paul.
claims.source: A. Milavec (2003); K. Niederwimmer, The Didache (1998).

claims.claim: Hilarion's letter (1 BC): keep a boy, cast out a girl.
claims.source: P.Oxy. IV 744.

claims.claim: Tacitus found it odd that Jews raised all their children; Musonius Rufus opposed exposure.
claims.source: Tacitus, Histories V.5; Musonius Rufus, Lecture 15.

claims.claim: Antonine plague 165-about 180; plague of Cyprian about 249-262.
claims.source: K. Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017).

claims.claim: Dionysius's plague letter, quoted verbatim.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History VII.22.7, 10, tr. McGiffert (file .cache/texts/url/first-christians-eusebius-7.txt).

claims.claim: Julian complained that Christians support pagan poor too.
claims.source: Julian, Letter 22 to Arsacius (362).

claims.claim: Stark: basic nursing could greatly cut plague mortality.
claims.source: Stark (1996), ch. 4; criticised as speculative.

claims.claim: Lawrence martyred August 258 under Valerian, days after Sixtus II (6 August); treasures story in Ambrose; gridiron in Prudentius; likely beheaded.
claims.source: Cyprian, Letter 80; Ambrose, De officiis II.28.140; Prudentius, Peristephanon II; standard hagiographical scholarship.

claims.claim: Didache 8: Lord's Prayer three times a day; fasts Wednesday and Friday.
claims.source: Didache 8 (Lightfoot).

claims.claim: Acts 19:19: books of magic worth fifty thousand pieces of silver.
claims.source: Acts 19:19.

claims.claim: Kreider's 'patient ferment'.
claims.source: A. Kreider, The Patient Ferment of the Early Church (2016) (title phrase).

claims.claim: Pliny governed Bithynia-Pontus about 110-112; letter X.96 about 112; Latin terms carmen, quasi deo, sacramentum, ministrae, superstitio prava et immodica, cibum promiscuum et innoxium.
claims.source: Pliny, Ep. X.96 (Mynors OCT 1963); A. N. Sherwin-White, The Letters of Pliny (1966).

claims.claim: Trajan refused a fire brigade at Nicomedia for fear of clubs.
claims.source: Pliny, Ep. X.33-34.

claims.claim: Hadrian's rescript to Minucius Fundanus (about 125).
claims.source: Justin, 1 Apology 68; Eusebius IV.9.

claims.claim: Tertullian's critique of Trajan's rescript.
claims.source: Tertullian, Apology 2.

claims.claim: 'Away with the Christians to the lion!' (quoted verbatim).
claims.source: Tertullian, Apology 40, tr. Thelwall (file first-christians-tertullian-apology.txt).

claims.claim: 'the blood of Christians is seed' (quoted verbatim).
claims.source: Tertullian, Apology 50, tr. Thelwall (file mae-tertullian-apology.txt); read in martyrs-and-empire.

claims.claim: Athenagoras lists the three charges; the Lyons martyrs (177) faced the same rumours; Polycarp's crowd cried 'Away with the atheists'.
claims.source: Athenagoras, Plea 3; Eusebius V.1.14; Martyrdom of Polycarp 9.

claims.claim: Fronto of Cirta made a speech against Christians.
claims.source: Minucius Felix, Octavius 9 and 31.

claims.claim: Octavius date between about 160 and 250.
claims.source: Standard introductions; relation to Tertullian debated.

claims.claim: Galen's comment on Christians preserved in Arabic.
claims.source: R. Walzer, Galen on Jews and Christians (1949).

claims.claim: Celsus, The True Word, about 177-180, preserved in Origen's Against Celsus (about 248).
claims.source: H. Chadwick, Origen: Contra Celsum (1953), introduction.

claims.claim: De Ste. Croix (1963) and Sherwin-White (1964) debate.
claims.source: Past and Present 26 (1963) and 27 (1964).

claims.claim: Nietzsche's view of Paul; Wrede called Paul 'the second founder of Christianity'; Bousset's Kyrios Christos (1913); Maccoby's The Mythmaker (1986) and the Ebionite story in Epiphanius.
claims.source: Nietzsche, The Antichrist §42 (1888/1895); W. Wrede, Paulus (1904), English Paul (1907); Bousset (1913); Maccoby (1986); Epiphanius, Panarion 30.16.6-9. PLEASE CHECK the Wrede phrase against the 1907 English translation.

claims.claim: Philippians 2:6-11 widely thought pre-Pauline.
claims.source: R. P. Martin, A Hymn of Christ (1997); debated.

claims.claim: Jerome (Commentary on Galatians, 386) thought Antioch staged; Augustine objected (Letters 28, 40, 82).
claims.source: As cited; J. Hennings, The Correspondence between Augustine and Jerome (1994).

claims.claim: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus (1870); Peter and Paul's feast 29 June.
claims.source: As cited.

claims.claim: Women's ministry: papal commissions on women deacons 2016 and 2020; Church of England women priests 1994, bishops 2015; Olympias deaconess about 400.
claims.source: Vatican announcements; Church of England; Palladius, Dialogue on Chrysostom.

claims.claim: Edessa annexed by Rome in the early third century; Christians there by the late second century.
claims.source: Chronicle of Edessa; S. Brock, standard surveys.

claims.claim: Armenia: Tiridates III and Gregory the Illuminator, traditionally 301, many historians about 314.
claims.source: Agathangelos; N. Garsoïan in The Armenian People I (1997).

claims.claim: Ezana of Aksum converted by Frumentius in the 330s; coins changed to the cross.
claims.source: Rufinus, Church History I.9; S. Munro-Hay, Aksum (1991).

claims.claim: Christian emperors made infanticide/exposure a crime in 374.
claims.source: Codex Theodosianus 9.14.1 (374); PLEASE CHECK whether the 374 law covers exposure or only killing.

claims.claim: Sunday holiday 321; Basil's foundation in the 360s-370s.
claims.source: Codex Justinianus 3.12.2; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43.63.

claims.claim: Gladiatorial games ended in the early fifth century.
claims.source: Theodoret, Church History V.26 (Telemachus); G. Ville; dates debated.

claims.claim: Theodosius made Christianity the official faith in 380.
claims.source: Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 (Cunctos populos, 380).

claims.claim: Koerbecke's Ascension (1456-57) from an altarpiece in Westphalia (the Marienfeld altarpiece).
claims.source: NGA object record; PLEASE CHECK.

claims.claim: Castel Sant'Angelo began as Hadrian's mausoleum and became a papal fortress.
claims.source: Standard.

claims.claim: The baldacchino at St Peter's stands over Peter's traditional tomb.
claims.source: Standard; the second-century 'Tropaion of Gaius' (Eusebius II.25.7).

claims.claim: Peter, Paul and others' living scholars' views (Wright, Hurtado, Dunn, Fredriksen, Boyarin, Wenham, Stark, Ehrman) are summarised in our own words from their named books.
claims.source: As listed in the lectures' refs.

flags: PLEASE CHECK the Didache text: it comes from the earlychristianwritings.com transcription of Lightfoot (1891). Its editorial verse numbers and curly braces round Scripture quotations were removed by script, plus one stray encoding mark in 4:15; no word changed. The CCEL copy (fetched by hard-cases) was not used because it has American spellings and a doubled phrase ('that hate you that hate you'), which suggests editing. A reviewer could check a few lines against the 1891 printed edition (archive.org).

Pliny (Gutenberg #2811): footnote markers [1066]-[1069] removed. The edition's typos 'officiate'' (stray apostrophe) and 'Secundtis' (for Secundus) are kept verbatim and explained in the context boxes.

Minucius Felix and Tertullian are New Advent's texts of ANF IV and III, 'revised and edited for New Advent by Kevin Knight': possibly light modernisation. HTML entities decoded. Tertullian's bracketed gloss '[i.e., the court of God.]' removed; the extract ends at 'but a curia'. One sentence of Octavius 9 (a crude charge) is cut, marked '…'.

PLEASE CHECK translator dates: R. E. Wallis (Octavius, published 1869/1885) and S. Thelwall (published 1869/1885) — death years not confirmed, though both published in the 1860s. A. C. McGiffert d. 1933; Lightfoot d. 1889; H. W. Fowler d. 1933, F. G. Fowler d. 1918; Melmoth d. 1799; Bosanquet's revision 19th century.
